a1.linkSameRegistry: the same registry as the directory sees it, with the schema
a1.linkIdentities: the identities on the other side of these
a1.dnDigest: — the identifier is too long for a readable RDN, so the cn is a digest of it
a1.filterPlaceholder: client_id, wtrealm, entityID, SPN or name
a1.filterHiding: The filter above may be hiding some.
a1.appearsFirst: One appears the first time a client_id, wtrealm, AppliesTo, entityID or service principal name is accepted here.
a1.fullerForm: The button opens the fuller form — the same action, with the PROTOCOL FAMILIES this application is declared for and a sentence about each, its per-protocol identifiers and its redirect URIs. It has no tab of its own in the sidebar because it is not a place in this console: it is the long way in from this page, and the row below is the short one. Both post here and reach one function.
a1.notConnected: For a relying party that has not connected yet. An entry usually appears because an identifier was ACCEPTED — a client_id at the token endpoint, a wtrealm on a sign-in response — and this is how to get one in ahead of that, which is what RFC 9700 mode needs if it is to judge a client against its own redirect URIs rather than against the oauth2.redirectUris setting. It records that it was created by hand, so it cannot be mistaken for one that turned up once and never came back.
a1.identifierTip: The key every protocol presents for this application: a client_id, wtrealm, AppliesTo, SAML entityID or Kerberos SPN. At most 512 characters, no line break.
a1.name: Name
a1.nameTip: What pages call it. With none, the identifier is the name.
a1.shortRowA: This row takes the identifier and a name and nothing else — it is the short way in for somebody already looking at the list. The Kind select that used to sit in it is gone for the reason
a1.shortRowB: gives at length: it asked the same question the protocol families do, in a vocabulary that does not line up with theirs, and it is DERIVED rather than declared — a kind is written when a protocol actually recognises the identifier. The fuller form is where the families, the per-protocol identifiers and the redirect URIs are, and an entry made here can be given all of them afterwards from its own page.
a1.oneEntry: One entry per identifier, whatever protocol brought it. The key is the identifier exactly as it arrived — not lower-cased and not namespaced by protocol — so an application appearing under one name in two protocols is one row with two kinds rather than two rows. That is the same rule that makes alice, her urn:uuid: subject and alice@REALM one person on the users page.
a1.countsOfChanges: Sessions and Users are counts of CHANGES, not of distinct sets. The ids themselves are deliberately not kept on the entry — an application used by two thousand people would otherwise carry two thousand values — so the count moves when the id differs from the last one recorded. Right for the ordinary case, and it undercounts somebody alternating between two applications.
a1.grantsNothing: An entry here grants nothing. Being in this registry does not let an application do anything it could not do before — this service issues a token to any client_id that asks. The one place it is READ is RFC 9700 mode (oauth2.rfc9700), which matches a redirect_uri against oauthRedirectUri by exact string comparison, decides public-versus-confidential from oauthTokenEndpointAuthMethod, and checks oauthClientSecret at the token endpoint. With that mode off, these entries are a record and nothing more.
a1.twoCredentials: Two attributes hold credentials — oauthClientSecret and appRegistrationAccessToken. Both are SEALED at rest wherever this process holds a durable key-encryption key, so this page shows their ciphertext; without one (development) they are in the clear. They are never written to the audit log.
a1.noDirectory: There is no embedded directory loaded in this process, so there is no ou=applications container to create an entry in and this form is not drawn. The applications registry has no store of its own on purpose — the directory IS the registry — so this is a build without ldap/ldap_server.js rather than a fault.
a1.theKey: THE KEY, exactly as the protocol will present it. At most 512 characters, and no line break: an entry whose cn would be longer than 64 characters is filed under app-<12 hex> instead, and appIdentifier is the attribute to search on either way.
a1.nameIs: The name is what pages call it; with none given the identifier is the name, because inventing a friendly name for an opaque id would be inventing a fact.
a1.noKind: There is no Kind to choose and that is deliberate. It used to be a select here, and it asked the same question the protocol families below do in a vocabulary that does not line up with theirs — eight kinds against fourteen families, five of which have no kind at all. It is also the wrong side of the line this registry draws: a family is DECLARED and a kind is DERIVED, written when a protocol actually recognises the identifier, so choosing one here was a form asserting a sighting that had not happened. Tick the families instead; the kinds fill themselves in as this application is used.
a1.landsIn: The entry lands in this realm's directory, at {container}
a1.oneRealm: . The console shows one trust realm at a time and this form writes the one it is showing — {realm} — because the realm is taken from the path this request arrived on. Applications are NOT shared between realms: an ldapsearch with that base DN is the same entry this creates, and another realm's registry has never heard of it.
a1.notSecondDoor: This is not a second door onto the registry. The form below posts to /admin/applications with action=create — the same action the list page's own Add an application row posts, calling the same function in applications.js that a protocol endpoint and an ldapmodify reach. Two forms over one function are two doors; there is one store behind them and nothing caches it.
a1.loadedHeading: The protected resource metadata that was loaded
a1.onEditableTab: The identifier, the name and the client_id are on the Editable fields tab above, filled in from the document: the name is its resource and the identifier is the client_id generated for it.
a1.familiesHeading: Protocol families it is declared for
a1.familiesNote: Tick as many as apply. The list is CLOSED — a value that is not one of these is refused rather than recorded, because a typo that silently became a new family is how one application comes to be declared for two spellings of one thing.
a1.colRecordedAs: Recorded as, when it turns up
a1.advancedView: Advanced view: every field an application has, for the families ticked.
a1.simplifiedView: Simplified view: the fields most applications need.
a1.switchTip: Draw the other view of this form. Nothing is created, and everything typed so far is kept.
a1.pfHint: Most fields depend on which families you tick above — a field appears when the protocol it belongs to is selected, so an OAuth client is not asked for a SAML entityID. Tick a family to see its fields. If you can see them all already, this browser does not support the :has() selector and the form is showing everything — nothing you type is affected either way, because the server reads what was posted and not what was visible.
a1.createdWith: It is created with zero counters and a description saying it was made by hand, so it cannot be mistaken for one that turned up once and never came back. You land on its entry.
a1.noKindRecorded: none — this service records no application identifier in that family
a1.prmHeading: Configure it from OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728)
a1.prmIntro: A protected resource publishes a JSON document describing itself — at {wellKnown} under its own host. Give this page that document and it fills in the form below: the resource becomes the default NAME, the permission base URI (oauthPermissionBaseUri) and the AUDIENCE of tokens issued for it (oauthAudience); scopes_supported becomes the permissions it exposes; a client_id is generated at random; and OAuth 2.0 is ticked. Nothing is created until you press Create, and every value can be changed first.
a1.prmUse: Use a protected resource metadata document
a1.prmOneWay: Give it ONE way. A document fetched from a URL is held to RFC 9728 section 3.3 — its resource must be the identifier the well-known URL was built from — which {mode, select, dev {this development-mode service reports and does not refuse} other {this product-mode service refuses}}. The fetch follows the federation outbound policy: no redirects, a size cap, a timeout, https with the certificate verified (plain http and a skipped check only in development mode){internal, select, yes {.} other {, and never to a loopback, private or link-local address.}}
a1.notRealmAs: not an authorization server of this realm
a1.asksIdentifier: a client asks for the identifier, not the scope
a1.signedNote: Shown so it can be read. This service holds no key for the resource to verify it with, and none of its claims were applied.
a1.onePerLine: one per line; empty removes the member
a1.asRead: The document as it was read,
a1.noScopes: The document names no scopes_supported, so the application is created exposing no permissions.
a1.fieldsOfForm: These are fields of the form below, whichever tab is showing: edit them here and press Create the application at the foot of the page. Everything else on the page below still applies.
a1.fIdentifier: The key this registry files the entry under. It defaults to the generated client_id, which is what a protocol sighting would file an OAuth client under.
a1.fName: What pages call it — the document's resource.
a1.fClientId: Generated at random, in the shape a dynamic client registration mints.
a1.fBase: The document's resource. A permission is this followed by its name.
a1.fAudience: The document's resource: the audience a token for this application carries. One per line.
a1.fPermissions: One per line, name or name|description, from scopes_supported with the resource prefix taken off. A scope that cannot be a permission is left out.
a1.fDetailsTypes: One per line, from authorization_details_types_supported (RFC 9396): the types a rich authorization request may name for this API. A line may be a JSON definition with a schema; openid_credential and a type another application declares are left out.
a1.fUrl: Where the document was fetched from. Recorded, never fetched again.
a1.membersA: What the document said, editable. The document stored on the entry as oauthResourceMetadata is the one you loaded with these edits applied; an emptied box removes that member.
a1.membersB: Changing a member here does not change the settings above: the name, base URI and audience were filled in from resource when the document was loaded.
a1.namesNoAs: The document names no authorization server. authorization_servers is optional, so there is nothing to compare with this realm's.
a1.allMatch: Every authorization server it names is one this trust realm publishes —
a1.unmatchedA: {u} of the {listed} authorization server(s) this document names {u, plural, one {is} other {are}} not one this trust realm publishes:
a1.unmatchedB: . The resource expects tokens from {u, plural, one {an issuer} other {issuers}} this service is not, at the address this page was reached on. You can still create the application; a token this realm issues for it will carry an iss the resource was not told to trust. This realm publishes
a1.thingsToKnow: {n} thing(s) to know before creating it:
a1.declaringA: Declaring a protocol family grants nothing, and in product mode it refuses the rest. The issuance policy refuses, in product mode, an issuance through a family the application is not declared for: an application declared for SAML 2.0 alone is refused an access token at /oauth2/token. In development the declaration is a RECORD OF INTENT — what this application is FOR — and refuses nothing, and an application declared for nothing at all is refused nothing in either mode. The configuration that DOES take effect is the attributes underneath: give the entry its redirect URIs, its grant types and its secret from
a1.declaringB: , and RFC 9700 mode judges the next request against them.
a1.declaredVsHappened: The families are DECLARED; appProtocol is what HAPPENED. Those two attributes sit next to each other on the entry and must not be read as one thing. This form writes the first; the second is accumulated by the protocol endpoints as they accept this identifier and is not editable here, for the reason every derived attribute on that page is not — a form that could rewrite it would make this console lie about the service's own behaviour, in a way indistinguishable from the recording being broken. The Applications drill-down shows both side by side, and says which of the declared families the entry has actually been recorded in.
a1.oneEntryRefused: One entry per identifier, whatever protocol brought it. The key is the identifier exactly as it arrives — not lower-cased and not namespaced by protocol — so this is refused if the registry already holds one under that name, and an application that appears under one name in two protocols is one entry with two kinds. Change what an existing one holds rather than creating it again.
a1.survivesA: This entry will survive a restart. An application here is a directory entry under ou=applications, and this process is running with persistence.mode={mode} — so it is written down along with every other application, person, group, federation relationship and SPIFFE registration. That is a property of the whole service and not of this page; see
a1.notPersistedA: Nothing here is persisted on this process. The entry is gone on restart, along with every other application, person and group in the directory. That is a property of the whole service and not of this page, and it is changeable:
a1.notPersistedB: writes the directory down, and is off by default.
a2.sealedTitle: The entry holds this encrypted under the key-encryption key — the same one this service's signing keys and the certificate authority are sealed with. An ldapsearch, an ldif file, a database row or a backup shows the ciphertext; this page opened it.
a2.operationalTitle: An operational attribute. A search returns it only when it is asked for by name (RFC 4511 section 4.5.1.8) — this dump shows it always.
a2.rdnDigestB: is longer than 64 characters, which is not a readable RDN. appIdentifier is the identity, not the cn.
a2.noDirectory: no directory is loaded in this process, so there is no entry and no registry
a2.name: Name
a2.enrollHeading: Certificates over ACME, EST and SCEP
a2.spMetadataB: and CONSUMES it: the document on samlSpMetadata, its AssertionConsumerService and SingleLogoutService endpoints as REGISTERED return addresses, its signing certificates as what its requests are verified against, its use="encryption" certificate on samlEncryptionCertificate, and its NameIDFormats, AuthnRequestsSigned and WantAssertionsSigned. A fetch that fails changes NOTHING, so whatever is registered stays in force.
a2.spMetadataC: shows what was consumed and takes an uploaded document.
a2.notConsumed: No metadata has been consumed yet.
a2.dialsAnything: This is one of two places in this service that dials anything at all.
a2.entryNote: Every attribute the entry carries — the operational ones and entryDN included, which a SEARCH would return only when asked for by name (RFC 4511 section 4.5.1.8) — with what each one is. This IS the entry — the registry is the ou=applications container and nothing caches it — so an ldapmodify shows here on the next refresh, and changes what RFC 9700 mode enforces at the same moment.
a2.noEntry: No directory is loaded in this process, so there is no ou=applications container and no entry to show. This module keeps no store of its own on purpose.
a2.oneAttrNote: These write the same entry an ldapmodify writes, through the same functions — the console is a set of controls in front of this registry and not a second copy of it. A change here is what RFC 9700 mode enforces on the very next request: add to oauthRedirectUri and that URI is accepted by exact match, set oauthTokenEndpointAuthMethod to none and the client becomes public, so PKCE is required of it and its secret stops being checked.
a2.wontChange: What these will not change, and why. The counters, the first and last sighting, the kinds and the protocols are DERIVED — they are what happened rather than what this application may do — and a form that could rewrite them would make this page lie about the service's own behaviour, in a way indistinguishable from the recording being broken. ldapmodify still reaches every one of them: an operator with an LDAP client is doing something deliberate, and refusing them HERE is the difference between offering an operation and merely not preventing it. appRegistrationJson is not offered either — edit the attributes beside it instead, which is what the registration is rebuilt from.
a2.takeOutHeading: Take it out of the registry
a2.revokeRegistrationNote: The entry and its history stay; the client_secret, the registration access token and the registration itself go. Afterwards RFC 9700 mode treats it as an unregistered, public client.
a2.noRegistration: It has no RFC 7591 registration to revoke — it is an identifier this service has seen rather than a client that registered, which RFC 9700 mode already treats as public.
a2.deleteEntryNote: The only control here that LOSES a fact: the entry goes and takes its {n} recorded authentication(s) with it. It will reappear, empty, the next time this identifier is accepted by a protocol.
a2.shownOnce: This is shown once; reveal it again to see it again. Asking is audited.
a2.registryAsDirectory: the registry as the directory sees it
a2.saveTip: Write this tab to the application. Nothing on the other tabs changes, and a refused value is shown with what was typed kept.
a2.familiesHeading: Protocol families it is declared for
a2.familiesNote: Tick the families this application speaks and press Save. A family ticked here adds its tab of fields beside this one, and its tab goes when it is unticked. In product mode a request through a family that is not ticked is refused.
a2.cfgNoteA: One tab per protocol, each with its own Save, beside the families this application is declared for. A tab of six fields or more opens on its simplified view, the fields an application usually needs; its advanced view shows every field, and a field the simplified view hides keeps its value when the tab is saved. Save writes what changed on that tab and nothing else: a single value is set, and an empty one is cleared; a list has the values taken out removed and the values put in added. A list shows one box per value, with + to add one and the bin to delete one; every box that is there must hold a value. The delegation lists on Every protocol open a search when you work in them — other applications, or the realm's groups — five results a page, each with an Add; appMayAct searches people or applications, and Use replaces its one value with the chosen entry's DN. A field with a fixed set of values offers them to choose from. These write the same entry an ldapmodify writes, and RFC 9700 mode reads it on the very next request. The web origins allowed to call it (CORS, appCorsOrigin) are not here: they are edited on the
a2.cfgNoteB: tab; nor are the roles a person must hold to use it (appRequiredRole), which are on the
a2.primaryTitle: The newest unexpired secret: the one this service signs and encrypts with, and the client_secret RFC 7591 and 7592 return.
a2.secretsNote: oauthClientSecret is what client_secret_basic, client_secret_post and client_secret_jwt authenticate with. The token endpoint CHECKS it in RFC 9700 mode and in product mode. An application may hold several (at most oauth2.clientSecretsMax, {max}), each with its own expiry: every unexpired secret authenticates, and the NEWEST unexpired one is the primary — the one this service signs HS256 ID Tokens and JARM responses with, keys symmetric encryption with, and returns as RFC 7591’s client_secret. A new value is minted here — oauth2.registeredSecretBytes random bytes, as a registration mints one — and never typed. The daily job oauth2.client-secret-expiry warns before one expires and removes expired ones, never the last one held.
a2.noSecret: This application holds no client secret.
a2.ratDescription: RFC 7592’s credential for reading and changing the registration — not a client secret
a2.atCap: It holds {n} secret(s), which is oauth2.clientSecretsMax. Remove one to add or rotate in another.
a2.emptyLifetime: Empty lifetime: oauth2.clientSecretLifetimeDays ({days, select, never {never expires} other {{days} days}}); 0 never expires. The existing secrets keep working.
a2.rotateNote: A new secret; every unexpired one goes on working for oauth2.clientSecretOverlapS ({s} seconds) and then expires.
a2.regenerateNote: Every secret it holds stops working immediately.
a2.collectIt: Collect it from the attribute table below.
a2.keepsOwnKey: The application keeps its own private key.
a2.noIssuer: none — it can authenticate, and cannot present an authorization grant
a2.noKeyPair: No key pair is managed for this profile. Issue one from this realm’s certificate authority, or upload a certificate the application already holds.
a2.replaceFromCa: Replace it with a key pair from this realm’s CA
a2.issueFromCa: Issue a key pair from this realm’s CA
a2.noCaA: This realm has no certificate authority yet, so there is nothing to issue a key pair from.
a2.buildOnPki: Build one on the PKI page
a2.chainPem: Chain (PEM, every intermediate and the root)
a2.takeOffNote: Not revocation: the certificate stays valid and this service stops accepting what it signs. The other profile’s key pair is untouched.
a2.regenerateKeyNote: Either way REPLACES the key pair on this entry. Issuing generates a new key pair here and signs it with this realm’s Issuing CA; the private key is sealed on the entry. Uploading registers a certificate the application already holds, and this service keeps no private key for it. A certificate from THIS realm’s authority may be uploaded alone. One from any other authority must come with its full chain — every intermediate and the self-signed root — and every link is verified: signatures, names, validity, and that each issuer is a CA allowed to sign. An upload carrying a private key is refused.
a2.registeredNote: , registered by value and verified beside the key pair above — replacing that pair leaves these alone. Change them with the attribute editor below.
a2.assertionNote: The RFC 7523 (JWT bearer) and RFC 7522 (SAML 2.0 bearer) sections are shown only for an application declared as OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect, because both profiles are used at the token endpoint. Declare one of those families under Protocol families to manage its key pairs here.
a2.alreadyCarriesB: material, and hiding the section does not take it off: the token endpoint still verifies what it signs. Its attributes are in the table below.
a2.credentialsNote: What this application authenticates and signs with: its client secret, and for each assertion profile the key pair this service manages beside the keys the application registered itself. The two profiles’ key pairs are separate on purpose — neither can sign for the other — so each has its own controls.
a2.mtlsHeldB: , and is held to it in every mode: a token request from it that does not authenticate by certificate is refused invalid_client.
a2.mtlsNotB: , so nothing here authenticates it yet. Set it to tls_client_auth (or self_signed_tls_client_auth) with the attribute editor below to use a certificate in place of a secret.
a2.noTlsCerts: This realm has issued this application no TLS client certificate.
a2.tlsAtMax: This application holds {n} valid TLS client certificates, which is pki.applicationTlsClientCertificateMax. Revoke one to issue another.
a2.issueTlsCert: Issue a TLS client certificate from this realm’s CA
a2.shownOnceDownloads: The private key is shown once, as downloads, and is not kept.
a2.mtlsNoCa: This realm has no certificate authority yet, so there is nothing to issue a TLS client certificate from.
a2.issuedItHeading: TLS client certificates this realm issued it
a2.implicitA: The implicit mapping for tls_client_auth: a certificate from this realm’s TLS client Issuing CA naming
a2.implicitB: , still listed here, authenticates this application with nothing registered. A certificate this service issued to anybody else never authenticates it, whatever subject is registered below.
a2.explicitA: The explicit mapping, RFC 8705 section 2.1.2: register one of these five, and a certificate whose chain verified against the client truststore (
a2.explicitB: ) and carries it authenticates this application. A DN is compared as a name, not a string. self_signed_tls_client_auth instead matches oauthTlsClientCertificateThumbprint
a2.explicitC: or a key’s x5c in its registered jwks.
a2.bindingYes: The main port is TLS, so every access token and refresh token issued on a connection that presented a client certificate carries cnf["x5t#S256"], and a resource server here refuses it on a connection without that certificate.
a2.bindingNo: The main port is not TLS (global.https), so no token can be bound.
a2.boundYes: : this application declared bound tokens, so a token request from it with no client certificate is refused in every mode.
a2.boundNo: : a token request with no certificate gets an unbound token.
a2.tipES256: ECDSA on P-256 with SHA-256: the default, and what most DID resolvers and wallets expect.
a2.tipEdDSA: Ed25519. Compact, and widely supported by DID tooling.
a2.didKeptNote: A key Generate made has its private half kept here, sealed under the key-encryption key, so this service can sign the Domain Linkage Credentials below. A key added to didPublicKeyJwk by hand has only its public half here. To change a key, generate a new one with replace ticked.
a2.linkageTip: Sign a Domain Linkage Credential for this origin with a kept DID key, and download the did-configuration.json to host at the address beside it.
a2.linkageNote: The DIF Well-Known DID Configuration: the file proves the DID and the origin are one party. It carries one Domain Linkage Credential, self-issued by the DID and signed with its key, and is good for oid4vci.domainLinkageLifetimeS (a year by default); download a new one before it expires.
a2.noLinkedDomains: No LinkedDomains service yet: add one to didService, such as LinkedDomains|https://app.example.com, to link the DID to an origin.
a2.didWebNote: did:web under this realm’s address: a resolver turns the DID into the document’s address above and fetches it from this service. The document publishes the keys, services and other names below. The DID follows the address this console is reached on; pin global.publicBaseUrl so it does not change with the host name.
a2.replaceTip: Take the keys already in the document off first, so the new key is the only one.
a2.generateTip: Make a key pair, add its public key to the DID document and show the private key once.
a2.generateNote: The public key is added to the document. The private key is shown once on the next page, and kept here sealed so this service can sign the Domain Linkage Credentials.
a2.keyIssued: Issued here — generated by this service and signed by this realm’s Issuing CA. The private key is on this entry.
a2.keyUploadedRealm: Uploaded — a certificate this realm’s own certificate authority issued. The application holds the private key; this service does not.
a2.keyUploadedExternal: Uploaded — a certificate from an external certificate authority, accepted with its whole chain up to a self-signed root, every link verified. The application holds the private key; this service does not.
a2.keyUnrecorded: A certificate with no recorded source and no private key here — written by hand, or by a build older than the provenance attribute.

a3.estBasic: EST: client id and secret {on, select, yes {accepted} other {refused}}
a3.overridesNote: The overrides are on the Certificate enrollment configuration tab; a value set there replaces the realm's.

a3.keyTip: The key pair this service generates for the certificate: its algorithm and size.

a3.addHostTip: Register the host name typed beside this for all three enrollment protocols.

a3.corsRemoveTitle: A page on {origin} stops being able to read this service's answers for this application on its next request.
a3.corsHeading: Web origins allowed to call it (CORS)
a3.corsIntro: These origins configure CORS on every published protocol endpoint of this service for this application — a browser page on one of them may read the answers to requests that name this application as their client, whatever the protocol. They are this entry's appCorsOrigin.
a3.corsNoClient: A request that names NO client — discovery, a JWKS, a DID document, a CORS preflight — is answered for an origin listed on ANY application in this realm, so an origin added here also lets that page read those. Empty allows no third-party origin, in both modes; this service's own origins and global.corsOrigins never need listing.
a3.corsNone: None — no page on another origin may read this service's answers for this application.
a3.corsOneOrigin: One exact origin — a scheme, a host and an optional port, with no path and no wildcard. It is stored normalised, so HTTPS://App.Example.com:443 is kept as https://app.example.com, and one that is not an origin is refused with the reason (STS-REG-0150).
a3.onePerLineAny: One per line; empty allows any.
a3.accessHeading: Access types this resource server owns
a3.accessIntro: The access-type catalogue: each type here is read by RFC 9396 authorization_details at the OAuth endpoints and by GNAP access rights alike, and a token carrying one is for this application. They are this entry's oauthAuthorizationDetailsType.
a3.accessNote: A type no application declares is refused by RFC 9396 in every mode, and by GNAP {dev, select, yes {only in product mode — this realm is in development mode, where it is granted as asked} other {in this realm, which is in product mode}} (the issuance policy's gnap-type-not-catalogued rule). For GNAP, interaction (always, default, never) and the actions that force consent decide whether the resource owner must see the approval page, and the authentication level is what their session must meet before it is drawn (#432 phase 6).
a3.helpType: Required. A type of the same name is replaced.
a3.helpDescription: Shown on the consent and approval pages.
a3.helpLocations: One absolute URI per line, beside this application's own addresses.
a3.helpRequired: Member names a right must carry, one per line.
a3.helpBearer: false refuses a bearer token carrying the type; empty sets no rule of its own.
a3.helpMaxLifetime: A token carrying the type lives no longer.
a3.helpDerivable: Types a right of this one may be derived from at RFC 9767 section 4, one per line.
a3.helpIntrospection: The person's claims this resource server is told at introspection, one per line.
a3.helpSchema: A JSON Schema every right of the type must meet.
a3.helpLimits: A JSON Schema (a subset: type, properties, required, bounds, enum, pattern, format) a right's limits must meet; none refuses limits.
a3.accessRefusedNote: A definition that does not read is refused with the reason (STS-REG-0294), and the type already declared stays.
a3.pauseTip: Stop delivering events on this stream. The receiver is told the stream is paused first; events are held, not dropped.
a3.enableTip: Deliver events on this stream again, held ones first. The receiver is told the stream is enabled.
a3.signalsNote: The CAEP and RISC streams this application created at /ssf/stream, matched by its identifier or its ssfReceiverId values. The members each shows are the ones its receiver set (SSF 1.0 section 8.1.1), so they are changed by the receiver and not here. Pausing or enabling a stream is the transmitter's act, and its receiver is sent a stream-updated event first. Every new stream starts from the defaults in the second table; change one in the field grid's Shared Signals group below.
a3.ssfNotLoaded: ssf/ssf.ts is not loaded in this process, so no stream can be listed.
a3.noStream: This application has created no stream yet.
a3.sentWithHeading: What its streams are sent with
a3.publisherNote: A statement whose iss is one of these is TRUSTED at POST /oauth2/register, verified against this application’s jwks or its RFC 7523 key pair from Credentials above. Add or remove an issuer with oauthSoftwareStatementIssuer in the attribute editor below. A statement this realm issued needs no declaration.
a3.noKeys: none — every statement from this issuer is refused
a3.noneIssued: This realm has issued no statement for this application.
a3.replacesShown: Replaces the one shown. The earlier statement still verifies until it expires.
a3.issuedNote: Hand the statement to whoever ships the software. A client that presents it is registered with the members it fixes, and they take precedence over the registration’s own JSON; whatever it does not fix, the registering client chooses — so fix grant_types and redirect_uris when those matter. software_id defaults to this application’s identifier. The iss is the issuer published at the address this page was reached on. It is not a secret, and it stops verifying when the realm’s signing key is replaced — in development mode, every restart.
a3.statementsUndeclared: RFC 7591 software statements are presented at the OAuth 2.0 registration endpoint, so this section is drawn for an application declared as OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect. Declare one of those families under Protocol families to issue a statement for it or name the issuers it vouches for.
a3.statementsNote: RFC 7591 section 2.3: a signed JWT of client metadata, presented at registration. In this realm a statement from an undeclared issuer is {req, select, yes {refused} other {accepted unverified}}, a trusted one {opens, select, yes {opens} other {does not open}} a registration endpoint closed to everybody else, and a registration {must, select, yes {must} other {need not}} carry one. Those are oauth2.softwareStatement* on
a3.markLeft: no longer on the entry; only the mark is left
a3.observedNote: Each address below is on this entry because a request NAMED it while the realm was in DEVELOPMENT mode, which believes any address and writes it down. Product mode refuses every one of them exactly as it refuses an address that is not on the entry at all{product, select, yes { — and this realm is in product mode now} other {}}. Confirm an address that really is this application's: the mark goes and the address stays. Discard one that is not: both go. Adding the address with the form below confirms it too. Addresses recorded before this service marked sightings carry no mark and cannot be told apart from registered ones — review the return-address attributes in the table above by hand before switching a realm to product.
a3.noneObserved: Nothing on this entry is marked as observed.
a3.grantToPlaceholder: part of an application name or identifier
a3.grantToNothing: No other application in this registry has a name or identifier containing that.
a3.danglingTitle: No application in this registry defines this permission — a deleted resource, a permission removed from under the grant, or an ldapmodify. Both console doors refuse to create one.
a3.doesNotResolve: nothing — the permission does not resolve, so this scope is treated as an ordinary one
a3.askedForTitle: This entry's oauthScope records having asked for this scope. Evidence rather than proof: it records what was requested, not what was issued.
a3.neverAskedForTitle: It has never asked for this one. A configured grant nobody has needed is exactly what this register is here to show.
a3.noIdentifierTitle: This application has no oauthPermissionBaseUri, and a permission is named by its base URI followed by its name — so no client can ever ask for this one. Set the base below and it resolves.
a3.noIdentifier: no identifier — this application has no base URI
a3.nothingHoldsTitle: Nothing holds it. That is the ordinary state of a permission that has just been defined — defining one grants it to nobody.
a3.permsWhichA: Which OTHER applications' APIs this one may reach, on behalf of whoever is signed in. The model is Microsoft Entra ID's: a RESOURCE application is given a base URI and exposes named permissions on it, and a CLIENT application is granted some of them. The grant lands on the CLIENT's entry — this one — as a value of oauthDelegatedPermission, because the client is the party that will name the permission in a scope.
a3.permsWhichB: is the whole register across every application, and
a3.permsWhichC: draws it; this is the one entry's part of it, where one half of every pair is settled by the page rather than chosen out of a list.
a3.permsScopeA: Then it asks for one as an ordinary OAuth scope. scope=openid https://example.com/write produces an access token audienced to https://example.com/ carrying scope: openid write — the base becomes the aud and the name becomes the scope, which is what a resource server wants: check the audience once, then read bare permission names. In product mode an ungranted permission is refused; in development it REFUSES nothing by default. With oauth2.delegatedPermissionsEnforced off — which it is unless somebody turned it on, on
a3.permsScopeB: — an ungranted permission is honoured exactly as a granted one is and merely recorded as ungranted.
a3.colTokenSays: What the access token will say
a3.holdsNone: It holds none. That is the ordinary state of an application nobody has granted anything to, and it changes nothing about what this service will issue it — until oauth2.delegatedPermissionsEnforced is set, an ungranted scope is honoured exactly as a granted one is.
a3.grantNote: The select offers every permission this service knows about EXCEPT the ones this application exposes itself and the ones it already holds. Its own are left out because a token audienced to the application that asked for it is what an ID Token already is, and app_permissions.js refuses that grant however it arrives; the ones it holds are left out because granting a value an entry already carries writes nothing.
a3.everyPermissionIs: Every permission defined here is either one this application exposes itself, one it already holds, or one with no identifier for a client to ask for.
a3.noApiYet: No application in this registry exposes an API yet. A permission must be DEFINED before it can be GRANTED, which is the one ordering rule this feature has.
a3.anotherExposes: Another application exposes one on its own Permissions tab, or on
a3.exposesNote: The RESOURCE half, configured here for this application only (2026-10-01): its base URI, the permissions it defines on it, and which OTHER applications hold them. Everything below is oauthPermissionBaseUri and oauthPermission on this entry, and oauthDelegatedPermission on each client's.
a3.sameRegister: is the same register across every application.
a3.exposesNone: It exposes none. Give it a base URI and define a permission on it, below.
a3.baseOneAnswer: The base URI is one answer per application and every permission it exposes hangs off it
a3.baseNone: . This one has none, so no client can ask for a permission it defines until it is set.
a3.baseTrailing: A trailing separator is added where there is none; clearing it leaves the permissions with no identifier.
a3.defineNote: The name ends up on the token's scope claim, so it must be a legal OAuth scope token (RFC 6749 section 3.3) and not contain |. It is defined on THIS application; to define one on another, open that application.
a3.name: Name
a3.grantsNoteA: Which other applications hold this one's permissions, one row per (client, permission). Granting here offers only permissions
a3.grantsNoteB: exposes, to any application but itself, found by a search rather than a list of every one; the grant still lands on the CLIENT's entry, so it reads back on that application's own tab as something it holds.
a3.grantedNone: No other application holds one of its permissions.
a3.searchAbove: Search for the application above and pick it; the grant form appears here with it chosen.
a3.noOtherApp: There is no other application in this registry to grant one to.
a3.nothingOwnYet: There is nothing of its own to grant yet: define a permission above, with a base URI set, and it can be granted here.
a3.appPermsNoteB: holds as itself, which its client_credentials tokens carry in the roles claim: a realm-wide role in every token, and an application's own role only in a token for that application. Delegated permissions, above, are what it holds on a person's behalf. Granting a role here is the administrator's consent; it is the same act as adding this application to the role on
a3.noRoleAdmits: No role admits an application that it does not already hold. Make one on
a3.resolvesBuiltIn: a built-in role, computed from the request rather than held
a3.resolvesNothing: nothing defines it — NOBODY can hold it, so everybody is refused
a3.stopRequiringB: . If it is the last one, this application requires nothing and everybody may use it again.
a3.requiredTip: appRequiredRole on this application's entry: the roles somebody must hold before anything is issued for it. Any one of them is enough; none means everybody.
a3.requiredHeading: Roles a person must hold to use it
a3.requiredNoteB: at all. Somebody must hold ONE of these roles before this service issues anything for this application — a token, an assertion, a WS-Federation response, a session. The user portal's Applications page lists it only to people who hold one, and a person who holds none is refused by the issuance policy and goes no further: nothing the rest of this page grants — permissions, scopes, the roles a token would carry — ever applies to them. Empty means everybody (the built-in EVERYBODY), which is how every application starts. These are the roles the application DEMANDS of others, stored on its own entry as appRequiredRole; the section below is the roles it HOLDS as itself, which is the opposite relation.
a3.requireFieldTip: A built-in role, a realm-wide role, or one of this application's own roles by its name inside it. Another application's role cannot meet this application's requirement, so none is offered.
a3.requireButtonTip: Add the chosen role to the roles this application requires. From the next request, somebody holding none of them is refused.
a3.everyRoleRequired: Every role that could be required already is. Make one on
a3.whoHoldsA: Who holds a role is decided on
a3.whoHoldsB: , which also lists every application that requires one and whether anything can satisfy it. The decision is the XACML issuance policy's, so a refusal's reason can be read on
a3.neverRecordedTitle: This service records no application identifier in that family, so no entry will ever carry a kind for it.
a3.declaredNoteA: Declared is appAllowedProtocol — what somebody said this application is FOR, on
a3.declaredNoteB: or through the Add and Remove forms below. Recorded is read off the KINDS in the table above, and not off the protocol labels beside them, because a federation partner is recorded under the protocol its relationship speaks and by label would be indistinguishable from an ordinary client.
a3.recordedNote: Recorded is not the same as "has authenticated". A kind is usually written when a protocol recognises the identifier — but a create takes one too, so an entry made by hand can be recorded in a family it has never connected in. The Authentications count above is the figure that answers whether anything has actually happened. And neither column grants anything: a family declared and not recorded is usually an application that has not connected yet, one recorded and never declared is the ordinary case, and nothing asks a protocol to check either — a mock that refused a protocol would remove a test case rather than add one.
a3.familiesNone: Neither list has anything on it. Nothing has been declared for this application and it carries no kind — which for an entry created by hand with no kind chosen is the state it is created in.
a3.claimsNote: The realm's claims are issued to this application, and its own are added to them; where both name the same claim, this application's value is the one issued. A row is a typed value, whose {placeholder} placeholders are expanded as on the realm's page, or a directory attribute of the person. The realm's rows are edited on the realm's page under Protocols.
a3.removeRowTip: Take this application's row off. The realm's row of the same name, if there is one, is issued again.
a3.noClaims: No claims: neither the realm nor this application configures any.
a3.pacTypeTip: The PAC claim type: string, int64, uint64 or boolean. A value that is not one leaves the claim out of the ticket.
a3.jsonTypeTip: The JSON type each value of a directory attribute becomes. A typed value is issued as written.
a3.nameFormatTip: The SAML 2.0 NameFormat of the attribute, such as urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:uri. Empty leaves it unspecified.
a3.namespaceTip: The SAML 1.1 AttributeNamespace. Empty gives the identity claims namespace.
a3.nameTip: The claim or attribute name. Setting a name this application already has replaces its row; a name the realm has is replaced for this application.
a3.valueTip: A typed value, with {placeholders}. Leave it empty and name an attribute instead to take the value from the person's directory entry.
a3.attributeTip: A directory attribute of the person, such as departmentNumber. Takes the place of the value.
a3.multiTip: Issue every value of the attribute, not only the first.
a3.setTipA: Set this row on the application. It is added to the realm's
a3.previewTip: Whose directory entry the values below are read from. Nothing is issued.
a3.noneInForce: No directory attribute is in force for this set, so
a3.noneInForceVc: a credential carries nothing but its subject identifier from this selection.
a3.noneInForceRows: it carries none — the rows above still go out.
a3.inheritedTail: ). Tick the boxes this application should carry instead and press Save; its selection then replaces the realm's for it.
a3.vcMetadata: The issuer metadata still advertises the realm's selection: it is one document for every client, so a wallet asking for a path is held to that and then given what this selection holds.
a3.saveSelectionTip: Write the ticked boxes as this application's whole selection for this set. It replaces the realm's for this application.
a3.useRealmTip: Take this application's selection off; the realm's is in force for it again.
a3.selectionNote: The realm's ticked catalogue of directory attributes, for this application. Unlike the rows above, which are added to the realm's and win by name, a selection is a whole set: once this application holds its own it REPLACES the realm's, so an attribute the realm ticks can be dropped as well as one added. A typed or attribute row above still wins over a selected attribute of the same name.
a3.lifetimesNote: Set an override in the field of that name below and press Save; empty it to take the realm's value again (Protocols → OAuth2 / OIDC → Token lifetimes). The clock skew, {skew}, is the realm's for every application.
a3.revealTipB: . Asking is an Admin Write act and is audited; the value is shown on the page that answers and is never put in a link.
sc.heading: Scope claims
sc.intro: An access token addressed to this application (as a resource server) on which one of its permissions was GRANTED carries the person's values of the directory attributes mapped to that permission, under the claim catalogue's names. Granting the permission is the grant of those claims, a standard OpenID Connect claim such as email included. They join the claims declared in oauthAccessTokenClaim and combine with the client's as oauthAccessTokenClaimsCombine says (Configuration tab); on a token for several resource servers only what every one wants goes in.
sc.noPermissionRest: , so there is no scope of its own to map. Define one on the Permissions tab (oauthPermission, under oauthPermissionBaseUri).
sc.noBaseUri: No base URI, so no client can ask for it yet.
sc.saveTip: Write the ticked boxes as the claims this permission carries.
sc.clearTip: Take the mapping off: granting this permission adds no claim.
sc.staleRest: These map nothing, and the next save on this tab drops them.
